name: Wen-ch'ang dialect of Hainan

catalog_citation: Hashimoto, Mantaro J. & Jerry L. Norman. 1971. A Guide to the Wen-ch'ang and Ting-an Dialects. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University, Chinese Linguistics Project. (ERIC ED 061 854 microfiche, 351 frames; archive.org)
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonological Description, sec. 2.4 Tones and sec. 2.5 Tone change, pp. 6-8 = ERIC frames 11-13 (the sentence 'Wen-ch'ang distinguishes the following seven tones:' closes p. 6 /; the tone table, the yang-ch'ü merger sentence, sec. 2.5 and the stress sentence are on p. 7 / / ERIC frame 12; the four sandhi examples open p. 8 / / frame 13)
catalog_quote: Wen-ch'ang distinguishes the following seven tones: [table] yin-p'ing rising 24; yang-p'ing middle level 33; shang high-falling staccato 53; ch'ü low falling 21; yin-ju high staccato 5; yang-ju middle staccato 3. Syllables carrying the shang tone are pronounced with a glottal stop ending, and the syllables are as a whole shorter than other legato tone syllables. The endings of two other tones, yin-ju and yang-ju, could be [p], [t], [k] or [ʔ]. The yang-ch'ü tone in Wen-ch'ang coalesced with either the shang tone or the yin-p'ing tone. 2.5 Tone change. A conspicuous tone change can be observed within ch'ü tone syllables in composite words; they are pronounced with a high level tone, though the same words in isolation are pronounced with a low falling tone. ʔiɛn12 'seal': ʔiɛn55-tuat5 'printing'. This change takes place only in syllables not occurring as final in a phonemic phrase. The final syllables of phonemic phrases never undergo the change described when those syllables carry the primary or the secondary stress: kan55-ʔbu53 'a cadre' but siu24-kan21 'a tree trunk'; ki55-miɛn24 'to meet' but mɔ24-ki21 'to see'.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wen-ch'ang Hainanese is a seven-tone language (yin-p'ing 24, yang-p'ing 33, shang 53 staccato, ch'ü 21, yin-ju 5, yang-ju 3). The only remark on stress is embedded in the tone-sandhi rule: the final syllable of a 'phonemic phrase' (tone group / compound) bears primary or secondary stress and keeps its citation tone, while non-final syllables are the sandhi (weak) positions (ch'ü 21 > 55). I.e. prominence is described as phrase-/compound-final, Southern-Min style; no independent word-stress rule is given. Hashimoto 1959 additionally transcribes toneless 'light-tone' (軽声, marked 0) particles, i.e. unstressed enclitic syllables exist.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentions 'the primary or the secondary stress' on phrase-final syllables without defining where secondary stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: Sandhi (and hence the stress remark) applies only to non-final ch'ü-tone syllables in composite words; Ting-an dialect 'has no tone sandhi' (p. 10/frame 16) and nothing is said about its stress. Sentence-final particles are written with neutral tone 0 in Hashimoto 1959.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonemic phrase' (compound word / tone group), not the morpheme-syllable; statement concerns citation vs. combination forms of disyllabic compounds.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Wen-ch'ang (Wenchang 文昌, 'Bon-shio/Bun-sio') dialect, the prestige variety of Hainanese (Glottolog lists Wenchang as a dialect under hain1238). The same 1971 guide's Ting-an (定安) section (analysis by J. Norman) says only 'Ting-an has no tone sandhi' and nothing on stress. Nakajima 2002 describes the Wanning (万寧) dialect and is silent on stress.
